QUESTION PRESENTED
Does the First Amendment apply to speech
regulation when the regulated speech constitutes
“treatment”?

INTEREST OF THE AMICUS CURIAE
Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF), a nonprofit law
firm, has defended individual liberty since 1973 —
including many appearances before this Court. 1  PLF
has a special interest in protecting  the rights of
professionals and workers to speak in the course of
their employment, whether that be mural painters
seeking to promote their artwork, 2 musicians trying
to earn a living doing what they love, 3 or doctors
sharing life-saving information with patients via
telehealth services.4  Indeed, the fate of several PLF
clients—both patients and telehealth providers—may
turn on the outcome in this case.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Access to information about healthcare can make
the difference between living and dying, flourishing
and withering.  Yet state regulators sometimes choke
off the supply of healthcare information, even when
patients are eager to receive it.  The Court’s approach
to this case will —quite literally —affect the live s of

1 No party’s counsel authored any part of this brief. No person
or entity, other than Amicus Curiae and its counsel, paid for the
brief’s preparation or submission.
2 Tilt Vision Studios, LLC v. The City of Waller, Texas, No. 4:23-
cv-03864, First Amended Complaint (S.D. Tex. July 26, 2024).
3 Barilla v. City of Houston , No. 4:20 -CV-00145 (S.D. Tex.
Jan. 15, 2020).
4 See MacDonald v. Sabando, No. 1:23-cv-23044, Complaint for
Declaratory and Injunctive Relief at 27 (D.N.J. Dec. 13, 2023);
see McBride v. Hawkins, No. 2:24-cv-01394-KJM-AC, Complaint
for Declaratory and Injunctive Relief at 1 (E.D. Cal. May 16,
2024).

2
millions of patients and families who rely on the free
flow of medical information.
Too often, courts confronted with the regulation of
healthcare professionals’ speech have given little
thought for the rights and interests of patients —the
very people most affected by restricting  healthcare
information.
Not only will this case have a profound impact on
patients, but the Court should take this opportunity
to clarify that the First Amendment protects patients’
and clients’ rights to receive information , as much as
it protects the rights of medical professionals to give
it.  See Ethan Blevins, Listening to the Listeners:  A
Patient’s Right to Receive Information via Telehealth ,
_ George Mason L. Rev. _ ( forthcoming 2025), SSRN
No. 5086249 5 (explaining how regulations of
communication between professionals and clients
interact with the right to receive information).
The right to receive information is a recognized
corollary to the right to speak.   The speech -conduct
distinction relied on by the Tenth Circuit here and
other circuits in similar cases neglects the interests
and rights of listeners.   The decision of the Tenth
Circuit should be reversed.

5 https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract
_id=5086249

3
ARGUMENT
I. The Outcome in This Case W ill Affect the
Many Patients Who Depend on Telehealth
This case will affect the regulatory environment
across the healthcare industry, particularly for
telehealth practitioners and their patients.
A. Jun’s Case
Telehealth saves lives.  It certainly saved Jun
Abell’s.  At eighteen months old, Jun was diagnosed
with a rare brain tumor.  See Cancer doctors and
patients fight for right to telehealth, Pac. Legal Found.,
https://perma.cc/DAA7-6YJJ.  Time was short.  His
parents arranged for treatment, and Jun’s dad waged
a multi-day war to save his son’s life by calling every
pediatric oncologist in the country he could find.  Ibid.
Chemotherapy and multiple surgeries failed to kill
the tumor.  But then Jun’s parents found Dr. Shannon
MacDonald, who works in Massachusetts.
Dr.  MacDonald specializes in proton therapy, an
innovative treatment unavailable at that time in New
York.  Ibid.
Jun’s parents consulted with Dr. MacDonald
remotely via telehealth, and the family decided to
start treatment under her care in Massachusetts.
That decision saved Jun’s life.  Ibid.
But Jun’s fight is not over.  He needs monitoring
for the rest of his life to guard against relapse.  But he
now lives with his family in New Jersey, a state that
forbids virtual doctor -patient visits with out- of-state
practitioners.  Ibid.
If Jun and his family had lived in New Jersey when
he’d first been diagnosed, the telehealth campaign

4
that saved his life might not have happened.  Yet even
now New Jersey makes it harder for Jun to consult
with the specialists most suited to watch over him.
Ibid.
Jun’s family is not alone.  People who suffer rare
diseases must often seek care outside their own state
or region because few specialists in the country may
know how to best care for them.  Without telehealth
options, they will have to face the burdens of regular
travel or forego essential care.
Dr. MacDonald and Jun’s family are now both
plaintiffs represented by PLF in a lawsuit challenging
New Jersey’s telehealth laws under the First
Amendment, among other theories.  See Complaint for
Declaratory and Injunctive Relief at 27, MacDonald v.
Sabando, No. 1:23 -cv-23044, 2025 WL 1367443
(D.N.J. Dec. 13, 2023). The district court recently
dismissed their complaint.  Id. at *16.  The case is now
on appeal to the Third Circuit.  This Court’s resolution
of this matter may determine whether Dr. MacDonald
can continue to help Jun via telehealth.
B. Shellye’s Case
The Court’s decision in this matter may also affect
the outcome in a telehealth case in the Ninth Circuit.
Shellye Horowitz lives in a rural coastal community in
northern California.  See McBride v. Hawkins, No.
2:24-cv-01394-KJM-AC, Complaint for Declaratory
and Injunctive Relief at 1 (E.D. Cal. May 16, 2024).
Like Jun, she suffers from a rare condition —a
bleeding disorder that requires specialized care.  No
such specialists live in her community.  Her
hemophilia specialist lives in distant Portland,
Oregon.  Telehealth would allow her to reach her
specialist despite the distance.  Instead, since

5
California prohibits physicians not licensed in the
state to offer care via telehealth to California patients,
she must make a 14-hour round-trip drive to even get
an oral consultation.
Despite Shellye’s rare condition, she is hardly
alone.  Rural areas often suffer from inadequate
access to healthcare even for those with more common
maladies.  See Linda J. Redford, Building the Rural
Healthcare Workforce:  Challenges—and Strategies—
in the Current Economy , 43 J. Am. Soc ’y of Aging 71,
71 (2019).  This problem has only grown thanks to an
ongoing physician shortage.  See Caitlin Styrsky et al.,
Restrictions to Care 1, Pacific Legal Foundation (May
2025).6  Experts have long touted telehealth as a vital
weapon in combating this sobering problem.  See
Redford, supra at 73.  This includes expanding access
to medical care as well as mental health care.  See
Bipartisan Policy Center, The Future of Telehealth
After COVID-19:  New Opportunities and Challenges
23–24 (2022).7
C. Dr. Sean McBride
Dr. Sean McBride is a nationally renowned
radiation oncologist specializing in genitourinary and
head and neck cancers.  See McBride, Complaint at 2–
3.  He works at a top specialty cancer hospital in New
York, but he has patients nationwide.  He often visits
with out-of-state patients virtually.  He has patients

6 Available at  https://pacificlegal.org/restrictions-to-care-howcollaborative-practice-agreements-for-advanced-practiceregistered-nurses-and-certified-nurse-midwives-limit-patientaccess/
7 Available at https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/future-oftelehealth/

6
in California, but he cannot advise and consult with
those patients via telehealth thanks to California’s
strict licensure rules.
Dr. McBride and Shellye Horowitz —represented
by PLF—have joined together to sue the state of
California.  Like Jun and Dr. MacDonald, they argue
that California’s rules banning out-of-state telehealth
violate the First Amendment.   See McBride,
Complaint.
Unfortunately, the federal district court dismissed
their legal challenge late last year.  In rejecting their
First Amendment argument, the district court relied
on the same reasoning as the Tenth Circuit in this
matter.  According to the district court, California’s
rules barring physicians not licensed in California
from consulting with patients via telehealth regulates
conduct, not speech, because such consultations “offer
treatment.”  See McBride, No. 2:24 -cv-01394-KJM-
AC, Order Granting Motion to Dismiss at 13 (E.D. Cal.
Nov. 19, 2024).  The case is now on appeal, and its fate
will depend in large part on the Court’s approach here.
II. The Right to Receive Information
Undermines the Speech-Conduct
Distinction
Patients have a right to receive information.  When
a medical professional speaks with a patient, the First
Amendment protects both the speaker and the
listener.  See Va. St. Bd. of Pharmacy v. Va. Citizens
Consumer Council, Inc., 425 U.S. 748, 756 (1976).  But
courts, including the Tenth Circuit here, have tended
to uphold regulations of professional -client speech on
theories that disregard the patient’s First
Amendment rights.  See, e.g., Chiles v. Salazar , 116

7
F.4th 1178 (10th Cir. 2024); Tingley v. Ferguson , 47
F.4th 1055 (9th Cir. 2022).
The Tenth Circuit’s reasoning focused only on the
professional’s right to speak, with no thought for the
right of the client to listen.   This neglect of listeners’
rights hurts patients.  This Court should reject the
Tenth Circuit’s speech -conduct reasoning, not only
because it violates the freedom of the professional to
speak, but also because it ignores the client’s right to
receive information.
Below, the Tenth Circuit held that a therapeutic
method involving only speech was subject to rational
basis review because the regulation forbidding that
speech was in fact a regulation of conduct given that
the speech was “treatment.”  See Chiles, 116 F.4th at
1206.  This holding departs from  this Court’s
traditional First Amendment jurisprudence, and the
Petitioner and other amici ably address the flaws in
the Tenth Circuit’s reasoning.  But that reasoning also
violates the underappreciated right of the client to
receive information.
A. Listeners’ Rights
“[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip
sides of the same coin.”  Conant v. Walters, 309 F.3d
629, 643 (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring).
This right to hear is alive and justiciable even when
the speaker lacks a First Amendment right to speak.
For example, in Lamont v. Postmaster General , 381
U.S. 301 (1965), this Court addressed a statute
requiring that incoming foreign mail deemed
“communist political propaganda” be detained and
released only upon the addressee’s request.  Id. at 302.
The postal service had intercepted a copy of the
“Peking Review #12,” addressed to Mr. Lamont, who

8
sued claiming a First Amendment injury.  Id. at 304.
Even though the foreign correspondent did not enjoy
First Amendment protection, this Court held that
Lamont had a First Amendment right as a listener.
See id. at 305 (“We conclude that the Act as construed
and applied is unconstitutional because it requires an
official act . . . as a limitation on the unfettered
exercise of the addressee’s First Amendment rights.”).
The concurrence went into greater depth:  “The
dissemination of ideas can accomplish nothing if
otherwise willing addressees are not free to receive
and consider them.  It would be a barren marketplace
of ideas that had only sellers and no buyers.”   Id. at
308.  Lamont and cases like it indicate that listeners’
rights stand independent from speakers’ rights.  The
right to receive information is  not a conditional right
that exists only when there is a corollary and
actionable right to speak.
This First Amendment right to receive information
has appeared in the healthcare context  as well .  In
Virginia State Board of Pharmacy v. Virginia Citizens
Consumer Council, Inc. , 425 U.S. 748, a consumer
group challenged a rule forbidding licensed
pharmacists from advertising drug prices.  Even
though the lawsuit was not made “by one directly
subject to its prohibition,” the consumers could defend
their own rights to receive information, since “the
protection afforded is to the communication, to its
source and to its recipients both.”  Id. at 753, 756.  The
Court struck down the advertising ban.  Id. at 773.
Likewise, the right to receive information arose in
a Ninth Circuit case involving doctor
recommendations t hat patients consume medical
marijuana, which at the time w ere unlawful under

9
federal marijuana policy.  Conant, 309 F.3d at 632.
While the majority only mentioned in passing the
patient’s First Amendment rights, Judge Kozinski’s
concurrence focused on the right to receive
information.  He agreed that the policy violated
physicians’ speech rights, but he felt the greater First
Amendment injury was to the patients’ rights to
listen:
[I]t is perfectly clear that the harm to patients
from being denied the right to receive candid
medical advice is far greater than the harm to
doctors from being unable to deliver such advice.
While denial of the right to speak  is never
trivial, the simple fact is that if the injunction
were denied, the doctors would be able to
continue practicing medicine and go on with
their lives more or less as before.  It is far
different for patients . . . .
Id. at 643–44 (Kozinski, J., concurring).
B. The Tenth Circuit Failed  to Recognize
Listeners’ Rights
The Tenth Circuit held that talk therapy is
“treatment” and therefore “conduct” under First
Amendment analysis.  This holding neglects the
therapist’s speech rights as discussed in other
briefing, but it also discounts a right that the Tenth
Circuit failed to even mention:  the right to receive
information.
A focus on the right to receive information reveals
a flaw in the speech -as-conduct approach taken by
cases like this one:  the listener receives less
protection when the information is targeted at the

10
listener, and more protection when the speech is
addressed to the public at large.
This problem is evident from the Ninth Circuit’s
reasoning in Tingley v. Ferguson , which the Tenth
Circuit embraced in this case.  Tingley, which involved
a therapy ban much like this one, adopted a
“continuum approach” to the speech -conduct
dichotomy.  At one end of the continuum is “public
dialogue,” which “receives the greatest First
Amendment protection,” and speech that arises in the
context of medical treatment is at the other end of the
continuum, where protections weaken.   Tingley, 47
F.4th at 1072– 73.  Hence, a doctor who publicly
advocates against COVID vaccines for children under
ten is fully protected, but if that doctor advises a
pediatric patient to forgo a COVID vaccine, then she
is not as protected.
This continuum results in a paradox:  the strength
of the listeners’ interests grows along the continuum
as the First Amendment protections weaken.  For
instance, if Ms. Chiles were to post her viewpoints
about mental health on social media, that speech is
fully protected, but if she were to express that same
viewpoint in a clinical setting to an individual client,
her speech would be unprotected.  Yet surely
Ms. Chiles’s client, who has sought her out for
counseling targeted at the client’s highly personal
needs, has a far greater interest in receiving that
information than the random social media user who
scrolls across Ms. Chiles’s viewpoints online.
Any given internet user has a right to hear
Ms. Chiles’s viewpoint, but that interest is abstract
and generalized.  Ms. Chiles’s clients, however, have
a concrete and specific interest because her speech is

11
targeted at the client’s circumstances and needs, and
the client has sought out her speech .  The result is
that listeners who have only a vague and generic
interest at stake enjoy First Amendment protection,
while listeners with a poignant and deeply personal
interest at stake enjoy little to none.  Under the Tenth
Circuit’s approach, the First Amendment protects
least the speech that affects listeners’ rights the most.
This continuum defies this Court’s precedents
regarding the right to receive information.  Under
Lamont, the degree of protection afforded to the
speaker does not affect whether the recipient of that
information is entitled to First Amendment
protection.  Thus, even if Ms. Chiles’s talk therapy
does not enjoy First Amendment protection, the client
would still enjoy the right to receive her therapy.  And
under Virginia Board of Pharmacy , recipients of
information have an actionable right to receive
information even if they are not the direct objects of
the regulation at issue.8

8 This Court should not hesitate to consider the right to receive
information just because there are no therapy patients before the
Court in this case.  This Court has often addressed the right to
receive information where only speakers were the parties bef ore
the Court.  See, e.g., Citizens United v. Fed. Election Comm’n, 558
U.S. 310, 339 (2010) (in a case brought by speaker, this Court
weighed “[t]he right of the citizens to inquire, to hear, to speak,
and to use information”); 44 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island ,
517 U.S. 484, 503 (1996) (in a case brought by regulated liquor
retailers, this Court struck down restrictions on liquor price
information because they “deprive consumers of accurate
information”).  A healthy marketplace of ideas is a key concern
in First Amendment analysis, see Virginia v. Hicks, 539 U.S. 113,
119 (2003) (reasoning that censorship violates the First
Amendment in part because it harms “society as a whole, which

12
Finally, viewing the Tenth Circuit’s reasoning
through the lens of listeners’ rights underscores  its
shortcomings.  From the listener’s perspective, the
Tenth Circuit’s amalgam of speech and conduct
disintegrates.  The Tenth Circuit reasons that “[t]alk
therapy is no less a medical treatment . . . simply
because it is ‘implemented through speech rather than
through scalpel.’”  Chiles, 116 F.4th at 1211.  But for
the patient or client, there is a big difference between
information (speech) and a scalpel (conduct).
Unlike hands -on treatment, harm caused by
doctor-patient or therapist -client speech is indirect
and depends on the listener’s agency.  See Va. St. Bd.
of Pharmacy, 425 U.S. at 770 (“[I]nformation is not in
itself harmful.”).  Any harm from faulty advice turns
on whether the listener accedes to the practitioner’s
judgment after engaging in their own informationseeking behavior.  See Edenfield v. Fane, 507 U.S. 761,
767 (1993) (“[T]he general rule is that the speaker and
the audience, not the government, assess the value of
the information presented.”).   When a scalpel slips,
the patient bleeds.  When a doctor gives bad advice,
harm to the patient is still only one of many
possibilities.  That is how any speech works:
information may lead to behavior that can be subject
to regulation, but until it does, it is still just
information—information that patients and clients
are entitled to hear.
This does not leave the state helpless to protect
patients and clients.  The state can respond to speech
it deems harmful with the storied instrument of its
own counter-speech.  See Whitney v. California , 274

is deprived of an uninhibited marketplace of ideas”), so the rights
of both speakers and listeners are ever intertwined.

13
U.S. 357, 377 (1927) (Brandeis, J., concurring) (“If
there be time to expose through discussion the
falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil by the
processes of education, the remedy to be applied is
more speech, not enforced silence.”), overruled on
other grounds by Brandenburg v. Ohio , 395 U.S. 444
(1969).  This is a vital distinction between hands -on
treatment and information about treatment:  the state
cannot easily place a shield between scalpel and skin,
but it can influence the health information
marketplace with its own public information
campaigns, informed- consent requirements, and
disclosures.  This approach has the triple virtue of
respecting the listeners’ right to receive information,
enhancing listeners’ interests by spoiling them with
more information, and promoting the state’s interest
in public health and safety.
None of this is to say that the government can
never curtail the right to receive information to
address concerns about manipulation and abuse of
vulnerable minors or other risks.   Just as with the
right to speak, the right to listen is subject to
exceptions and varying tiers of scrutiny.  See Blevins,
supra  (discussing limits and exceptions to the right to
receive information).
But this Court prefers more information rather
than the “highly paternalistic” approach of keeping
people in the dark for their own good.  Va. State Bd. of
Pharmacy, 425 U.S. at 770; see also Citizens United ,
558 U.S. at 361  (“[I]t is our law and our tradition that
more speech, not less, is the governing rule.”).  Courts
should instead recognize “that people will perceive
their own best interests if only they are well enough
informed, and that the best means to that end is to
open the channels of communication rather than to

14
close them.”  Va. St. Bd. of Pharmacy, 425 U.S. at 770;
see also 44 Liquormart, 517 U.S. at 503 (“The First
Amendment directs us to be especially skeptical of
regulations that seek to keep people in the dark for
what the government perceives to be their own
good.”).  The state can rebut this presumption; if Ms.
Chiles’s controversial therapy pose s a serious risk of
harm to minors, the government should carry the
burden to prove it.
CONCLUSION
Patients have a right to seek out and receive
information vital to their welfare and survival.  The
Tenth Circuit has imperiled that right.  This Court
should reverse.
Respectfully submitted,
 ETHAN W. BLEVINS
  Counsel of Record
CALEB R. TROTTER
